input.currentSkills: Survey design, customer interviews, data analysis in Excel, writing, stakeholder communication

starting_point.summary: Several things you have done in your marketing coordinator role overlap with activities in UX research work, particularly customer interviews, survey design, and stakeholder communication. The question is not whether these transfer at all, but how closely your specific experience matches what a given employer is looking for.
important_unknowns: What kind of work a specific target role actually requires — this varies enough by company, team, and seniority that an actual job posting would replace these general observations with that employer's specifics.

What your data analysis in Excel involved — the type of data, the purpose, and the depth of analysis are not established by what you supplied, so how well it transfers to research analysis is unclear.
Whether your customer interviews were conducted in a way that resembles UX research interviewing — the context, goals, and methods you used are not described, so the degree of overlap is uncertain.

transferable_strengths.evidence: You supplied that you have conducted customer interviews in your marketing coordinator role.
transferable_strengths.transfer: Experience conducting customer interviews may carry over to UX research interviewing, particularly in comfort with conversation, question preparation, and drawing out responses — though how closely your approach resembles research-oriented interviewing depends on specifics you have not described.

transferable_strengths.evidence: You supplied that survey design is part of your experience.
transferable_strengths.transfer: Survey design is a method used in UX research, so this experience may carry over — though the extent depends on what types of questions you wrote, what the surveys were intended to measure, and how results were used.

transferable_strengths.evidence: You supplied data analysis in Excel as part of your experience.
transferable_strengths.transfer: Familiarity with organizing and analyzing data may carry over to research analysis tasks, though what kinds of data and analysis you have done is not established, so the degree of transfer is unclear.

transferable_strengths.evidence: You supplied stakeholder communication as part of your four years in a B2B SaaS marketing role.
transferable_strengths.transfer: Experience communicating across stakeholders may carry over to presenting or discussing research findings with product, design, or business partners, depending on what those roles expect.

transferable_strengths.evidence: You supplied writing as part of your experience.
transferable_strengths.transfer: Writing experience may carry over to research documentation, discussion guides, and presenting findings in written form — the specific application would depend on what the role requires.

start_here.why_it_matters: You have customer interview experience, which means this is an adjacent area rather than a blank starting point. Comparing your current approach against what UX research roles ask for gives you something concrete to build from and compare against.
start_here.current_evidence: You supplied that you have conducted customer interviews, but what goals guided them, how you structured them, and what you did with the findings is not established.
start_here.gap: UX research interviewing may involve specific orientations around uncovering behavior, needs, or mental models rather than marketing objectives — whether your interview approach already reflects any of this is not established by what you supplied.
start_here.next_move: Compare how you currently structure and conduct interviews against descriptions of research-oriented interviewing in several credible sources or real job postings.
start_here.proof: A written comparison of your current interview approach against what you find in role descriptions or credible sources — noting where your practice overlaps and where it differs — that you can revisit as you apply to specific roles.

next_move.primary: If you have not documented how you conduct customer interviews, write a short description of what you typically do — how you prepare, what kinds of questions you ask, and what you do with what you learn. Then compare that description against three to five UX researcher job postings to see where the language and expectations overlap with your experience and where they do not.
next_move.why: This gives you a concrete artifact grounded in your actual experience to compare against real role requirements, which is more actionable than studying the field in the abstract.
next_move.proof: A written description of your interview approach alongside notes on where it aligns with and diverges from the postings you reviewed — a document you can refine and refer back to.
alternatives: If you have a past survey you designed, review it against the goals and structure described in UX research resources and note what you would change — this surfaces your current instincts and where they may need development.

If you have written reports or summaries based on customer data, document one example of your analytical process and output, then compare it to examples of research readouts described or shown in public UX research resources.

skill_gaps.target_relevance: May be relevant to UX researcher roles that involve moving from raw interview or survey data to patterns, themes, or findings that inform decisions.
skill_gaps.current_evidence: You supplied data analysis in Excel and writing, which may involve some form of synthesis, but the nature of that work is not established.
skill_gaps.gap: Whether your analysis and writing experience extends to identifying patterns across qualitative data and articulating them as research findings is not established.
skill_gaps.next_move: Review public examples of UX research readouts or synthesis artifacts and compare them to the kinds of outputs you have produced — note the differences in structure and reasoning.
skill_gaps.proof: A written synthesis of a small set of interview notes or survey responses — even from a past project — organized into themes with a short explanation of what they suggest.

skill_gaps.target_relevance: May be relevant where UX researcher roles involve scoping a research effort — defining questions, choosing methods, and planning logistics — before any data is collected.
skill_gaps.current_evidence: You supplied survey design experience, which may include some planning, but the extent to which you have scoped a research effort from the question-definition stage is not established.
skill_gaps.gap: Defining a research question, selecting an appropriate method, and planning a study end-to-end may go beyond what your supplied experience establishes.
skill_gaps.next_move: Draft a research plan for a question you are genuinely curious about — one that specifies the question, the method you would use, and why.
skill_gaps.proof: A written research plan document you can review, critique, and potentially show as an example of your thinking.

skill_gaps.target_relevance: May be relevant where researchers present findings in a way that informs decisions by product, design, or business partners.
skill_gaps.current_evidence: You supplied stakeholder communication experience in a B2B SaaS marketing role, which is related, but whether it involved presenting data-driven findings in a structured format is not established.
skill_gaps.gap: Presenting research findings — structuring what you learned, what it means, and what it suggests — may differ from the stakeholder communication you have done, depending on its nature.
skill_gaps.next_move: Take one past customer insight or data point from your marketing work and write it up as if you were presenting it to a product team — what the finding was, what it suggests, and what you are uncertain about.
skill_gaps.proof: A short written or slide-based findings summary grounded in something you have actually observed or analyzed.

skill_gaps.target_relevance: May be relevant if your target roles involve methods beyond interviewing and surveying — such as usability studies, diary studies, or observational research.
skill_gaps.current_evidence: You supplied customer interviews and survey design, which are two qualitative and mixed methods — other methods are not established.
skill_gaps.gap: Awareness of a broader range of research methods and the reasoning behind choosing one over another is not established by what you supplied.
skill_gaps.next_move: Read through the methods sections of several UX researcher job postings and identify which methods appear most often, then investigate what each involves.
skill_gaps.proof: A personal reference document listing the methods you encountered, a plain-language description of each, and notes on which ones appear in roles you are considering.

skill_gaps.capability: Translating business questions into research questions
skill_gaps.target_relevance: May be relevant if your target roles expect researchers to take a business or product question and reframe it into something researchable — a distinct reasoning step.
skill_gaps.current_evidence: You supplied four years in B2B SaaS marketing with stakeholder communication and writing, which may involve translating business context — but whether this extends to research question framing is not established.
skill_gaps.gap: Reframing a product or business question into a specific, answerable research question is not established by what you supplied.
skill_gaps.next_move: Pick a real business question from your current role and write two versions of it — one as a business goal and one reframed as a question you could answer through interviews or a survey.
skill_gaps.proof: A written pair of statements showing the original business question and your research reframe, with a short note on how you made the translation.

role_expectations_to_check.question: Worth verifying: whether the role expects a formal UX research portfolio with documented case studies, or whether demonstrated research outputs in another form are acceptable.
role_expectations_to_check.why_it_matters: If a portfolio is a hard requirement, building one becomes a prerequisite before applying, which materially shapes where your time goes first.
role_expectations_to_check.how_to_verify: Check several active job postings for UX Researcher roles at your target company size and stage, and look specifically for what application materials are requested.

role_expectations_to_check.question: Worth verifying: how much of the role is generative research (discovery, concept testing) versus evaluative research (usability testing), since the balance varies significantly across teams.
role_expectations_to_check.why_it_matters: Your supplied experience maps more directly to generative methods; a role weighted toward usability testing may involve methods you have less direct experience with.
role_expectations_to_check.how_to_verify: Job postings that list specific study types or deliverables will tell you more than generic descriptions — look for phrases like 'usability testing,' 'concept validation,' or 'diary studies.'

role_expectations_to_check.question: Worth verifying: whether familiarity with particular research planning, synthesis, or testing tools is expected, since the specific tools vary by team and are often listed in postings.
role_expectations_to_check.why_it_matters: If specific tools appear consistently across postings you are targeting, knowing which ones lets you decide whether to get hands-on experience before applying.
role_expectations_to_check.how_to_verify: Scan the tools or software sections of multiple postings for the same role title across different companies and note which names recur.

role_expectations_to_check.question: Worth verifying: whether the role sits embedded in a product team, in a central research function, or as a consultant to multiple teams, since this affects the degree of autonomy and the type of stakeholder relationships involved.
role_expectations_to_check.why_it_matters: Your stakeholder communication experience is more directly relevant if the role requires ongoing cross-functional collaboration; a more isolated research function would draw on different parts of that background.
role_expectations_to_check.how_to_verify: Look for language like 'embedded,' 'centralized,' 'research ops,' or 'partner with product and design' in the responsibilities section of postings.

transition_tasks.task: Identify UX researchers, including those working in B2B SaaS if possible, and ask about how the role is structured in their companies and what preparation they found valuable before starting.
transition_tasks.why: Your background is specifically B2B SaaS, and researchers in that context may have useful perspective on how your marketing and customer interview experience is typically received.

transition_tasks.task: Gather and document any work samples from your marketing role — survey materials, notes from interview processes, or analysis you have done — and review them against the kinds of artifacts described in UX researcher job postings to see where your work aligns and where it differs.
transition_tasks.why: You have supplied experience that may already constitute research evidence; making it legible in UX research terms addresses the portfolio question before you have completed new projects.

transition_tasks.task: Collect and compare at least five active job postings for UX Researcher roles that match your target company type, and note which requirements appear consistently versus occasionally.
transition_tasks.why: With limited hours per week, knowing which capabilities appear across most postings versus only some helps you direct effort toward the gaps most likely to matter for the roles you will actually pursue.

directions.why_it_connects: The visitor has run a user interview and listed user research as an explicit interest, and their cross-functional collaboration with product and design means they have worked alongside this function from the engineering side.
directions.what_the_work_involves: Depending on the organization, this kind of role can involve planning and conducting interviews, usability studies, or surveys, synthesizing findings into insights, and presenting those to product and design teams to inform decisions. Some versions are embedded in product teams; others sit in a centralized research function.
directions.worth_learning_more_about: How much of this role, in the kinds of organizations you are considering, involves designing and running studies versus synthesizing and communicating findings to stakeholders who then act on them independently?
directions.one_way_to_investigate: Read 10-15 current job postings for 'UX researcher' and 'user researcher' across different company sizes, and note what methods, deliverables, and collaboration structures they describe — the variation will tell you more than any general overview.

directions.why_it_connects: The visitor has written specs, collaborated cross-functionally with product and design, and stated an interest in strategy and business impact — all directly relevant to what technical PM roles involve on the coordination and scoping side — and their backend API and system design background means they can engage with engineering trade-offs from first-hand experience.
directions.what_the_work_involves: This kind of role can involve defining what gets built and why, working with engineers on feasibility, writing requirements or product briefs, and connecting technical decisions to business outcomes. Some versions are heavily engineering-facing; others split time between customers, stakeholders, and the development team.
directions.worth_learning_more_about: In the specific types of products and organizations you are drawn to, how much influence does the PM role have over strategic direction versus translating a strategy that others have set?
directions.one_way_to_investigate: Find first-person accounts from engineers who moved into technical PM roles — blog posts, forum threads, or short conversations — and ask specifically about what day-to-day decision authority looks like versus what they expected going in.

directions.why_it_connects: The visitor's backend Python, API, and system design experience gives them direct technical grounding in the kinds of integrations and architecture questions this role addresses, and their cross-functional collaboration and spec-writing suggest comfort translating between technical and non-technical stakeholders.
directions.what_the_work_involves: This kind of role can involve working with prospective or existing customers to understand their technical environment, demonstrating how a product fits their needs, building proof-of-concept integrations, and acting as a bridge between the sales or customer-facing side and the engineering team. The balance between customer interaction and hands-on technical work varies considerably by company.
directions.worth_learning_more_about: How much of this role, at the organizations you would consider, involves independent technical work versus being present in and responsive to a sales cycle driven by others?
directions.one_way_to_investigate: Look at job postings for 'solutions engineer' and 'sales engineer' at companies whose products you already use or understand technically, and compare what each lists as day-to-day responsibilities versus success metrics.

directions.why_it_connects: The visitor has stated an explicit interest in strategy and business impact, and their SQL experience and system design background both point toward comfort with structured data and reasoning about how systems connect — capabilities that can be relevant to analytical and operational roles focused on business problems.
directions.what_the_work_involves: Depending on the organization, this kind of work can involve analyzing operational or business data to surface insights, building models or frameworks to support decisions, and working with leadership or cross-functional partners on how to act on findings. current_salary_range.note: Higher end requires 4+ years experience or a mid-size market; entry-level coordinators in smaller metros often land at $42–48K.

target_salary_range.note: Entry-level PM salaries cluster near $70–80K outside FAANG; startup PMs may earn less cash but receive equity that could be worthless.

salary_delta.realistic_starting_salary: A career-changer landing their first PM role in 2026 without a CS background or MBA should realistically target $68–75K, not the $82K midpoint, especially at companies below 500 employees.

transition_costs.item: Product management certificate (e.g., Product School, Reforge, or Pragmatic Institute)
transition_costs.note: Not a hiring requirement at most companies, but signals commitment to interviewers who will otherwise question why a marketer can handle roadmapping and technical scoping.

transition_costs.item: Books and self-study materials (Inspired, Shape Up, Continuous Discovery Habits, etc.)
transition_costs.note: Interview loops for PM roles test product sense and frameworks directly; showing up without this knowledge is disqualifying.

transition_costs.item: Side project or portfolio work (domain hosting, tools, design software subscriptions)
transition_costs.note: Hiring managers expect a portfolio or case study since you lack shipped-product experience; this signals initiative and gives interview material.

transition_costs.item: Networking and informational interviews (travel, coffee meetings, LinkedIn Premium ~6 months)
transition_costs.note: Most PM hires happen through warm referrals, not cold applications; this is not optional if you want a 6-month timeline to be realistic.

transition_costs.item: Income gap during active job search (assumes 2–3 months of reduced freelance/part-time work to interview)
transition_costs.note: PM interview processes average 4–8 weeks per company and often require take-home assignments; most candidates reduce work hours and absorb the income hit.
Useful if you have no internal advocate to review PM-specific framing of your marketing experience.

roi_analysis.year_3_cumulative: Assuming a $20K annual raise held and modest PM progression, you recoup transition costs in roughly 6 months and net approximately $51K more over 3 years after subtracting the $9,350 in costs.
roi_analysis.year_5_cumulative: If you earn one promotion to mid-level PM by year 3 (realistic), cumulative earnings advantage over staying in marketing reaches approximately $120–140K over 5 years.

output.negotiation_leverage: Your marketing background is genuinely differentiable — most PMs lack fluency in user messaging, go-to-market coordination, and campaign analytics, so lean hard on that in B2C or growth-focused roles where those skills directly map to PM responsibilities.
output.financial_warning: The 6-month timeline is aggressive for a career-changer with no shipped product experience; if the search stretches to 10–12 months (which is common), the income gap cost nearly doubles and payback period extends past year 1 — plan your cash reserves accordingly.

skillGaps.capability: Working with engineering on scope and feasibility
Communicating product strategy to varied audiences

first.focus: Start with user research and discovery, because it is the foundation the other gaps build on — structuring tradeoffs and defining metrics both require knowing what you learned from users and why it matters. Your marketing background gives you real exposure to audiences and messaging, which overlaps with research thinking.
first.how_youll_know: You can take a specific product or feature you already know well, write down three distinct user problems it might solve, and then explain — in plain language, without marketing framing — which one you would prioritize investigating first and why the others can wait.

then.focus: Move to structuring product decisions with tradeoffs, using what you learned in the first phase as your raw material — practice making a real or realistic decision where you have to weigh user needs against constraints you name explicitly.

later.focus: Working with engineering on scope and feasibility, and defining and tracking product metrics, can develop in parallel once the earlier two are underway — both benefit from having a concrete decision-making framework in place first. Communicating product strategy is a useful gap to address through the work itself: practice explaining decisions you have already made in the earlier phases to someone outside product.

output.plateau_note: The fix when you feel stuck: find or create one small, low-stakes product problem you can own all the way through, even outside a formal job context.
